articles.title: Quando gli anni novanta diventarono il passato
articles.summary: Melissa Auf der Maur è stata la bassista delle Hole e degli Smashing Pumpkins, ma ora un libro rivela la sua passione per la fotografia e racconta in maniera intima anche un’epoca significativa nella storia del rock
articles.preview: Metà anni novanta, in un baraccio di Los Angeles frequentato da musicisti e artisti per scaricare l’adrenalina della serata o semplicemente per non andare a dormire, Michael Stipe dei R.E.M. chiede alla ragazza dai lunghi capelli rossi che è seduta accanto a lui perché mai passi così tanto tempo a fotografare la gente. Lei risponde che in caso arrivassero gli alieni e si chiedessero come fosse essere una donna in una rock band della fine del novecento avrebbero tutta la documentazione necessaria.
articles.body:
Metà anni novanta, in un baraccio di Los Angeles frequentato da musicisti e artisti per scaricare l’adrenalina della serata o semplicemente per non andare a dormire, Michael Stipe dei R.E.M. chiede alla ragazza dai lunghi capelli rossi che è seduta accanto a lui perché mai passi così tanto tempo a fotografare la gente. Lei risponde che in caso arrivassero gli alieni e si chiedessero come fosse essere una donna in una rock band della fine del novecento avrebbero tutta la documentazione necessaria. Quella ragazza dai lunghi capelli rossi si chiama Melissa Auf der Maur e in quel momento è la bassista delle Hole, la band di Courtney Love.

Oggi Auf der Maur ha raccolto tutte quelle foto nel libro My ’90s rock photographs, pubblicato da Del Monico Books in occasione di una mostra all’Art gallery of Ontario di Toronto. Nella conversazione con Stipe che accompagna il volume, la musicista torna su quella serata a Los Angeles e osserva che oggi l’aliena si sente lei. Il mondo in cui viviamo, sempre più connesso e dipendente dalle macchine, le sembra lontanissimo da quello che aveva fotografato negli anni novanta.

Quel decennio è finito da poco più di un quarto di secolo. Eppure certe immagini dell’epoca sembrano arrivare da un passato più remoto di quelle degli anni ottanta, un periodo che la cultura pop continua ossessivamente a citare, campionare, riciclare e reinventare. Alcuni aspetti degli anni ottanta come la fascinazione per i super ricchi, la demonizzazione della povertà, la feticizzazione della tecnologia, quel senso di paranoia per la fine del mondo e una certa disperata, inspiegabile frivolezza, appartengono più che mai all’epoca incasinata in cui viviamo.

Gli anni novanta, invece, almeno quelli che vediamo nelle fotografie di Auf der Maur, sembrano invece appartenere a un mondo che non esiste più. Molto più antico anche se posteriore e molto più misterioso anche se così vicino a noi.

Melissa Auf der Maur è nata a Montréal, in Canada, nel 1972 e ha studiato fotografia alla Concordia university. Suonava il basso in una band chiamata Tinker quando, nel 1994, Billy Corgan degli Smashing Pumpkins la segnalò a Courtney Love, che cercava una nuova bassista per le Hole dopo la morte per overdose di Kristen Pfaff.

Auf der Maur entrò così in una delle band più importanti e turbolente del rock alternativo statunitense. Rimase nelle Hole fino al 1999, poi passò per un breve periodo negli Smashing Pumpkins. Nel suo memoir Even the good girls will cry Auf del Maur scrive che le Hole erano state la sua laurea in umanità – humanity, con un gioco di parole sulle humanities, le materie umanistiche – e gli Smashing Pumpkins il suo master in musica.

Vite incontenibili

Prima di diventare una musicista famosa, Auf der Maur voleva fare la fotografa. Quando Courtney Love le propose di entrare nelle Hole, la sua prima reazione fu di rifiutare: aveva intenzione di continuare l’università. Alla fine accettò, ma non abbandonò mai la macchina fotografica. Anzi, fotografare diventò un modo per conservare qualcosa di sé mentre la sua vita cambiava a una velocità impressionante. Da studente si trovò da un giorno all’altro a essere una rockstar.

Le fotografie raccolte nel libro non sono i soliti ritratti di rockstar scattati da un professionista con un pass per il backstage. Auf der Maur era parte di quel mondo, condivideva con gli altri musicisti gli alberghi, i lunghi spostamenti in autobus, le feste e le interminabili attese in camerini puzzolenti prima dei concerti.

Courtney Love, Billy Corgan e Michael Stipe compaiono spesso nelle sue fotografie, ma non sembrano mai particolarmente interessati alla presenza della macchina fotografica. Sono amici, colleghi, compagni di viaggio. E poi ci sono anche tanti autoritratti.

Auf der Maur aveva cominciato a fotografarsi quasi ogni giorno quando studiava all’università e continuò a farlo durante i tour. La vediamo riflessa negli specchi dei bagni e dei camerini, seduta sui letti disfatti degli alberghi, circondata da vestiti, strumenti musicali e valigie aperte. Quegli autoritratti colpiscono perché sono antenati dei selfie, ma realizzati in un’epoca in cui fotografare se stessi era ancora una pratica soprattutto artistica e non un’abitudine quotidiana.

Sono immagini che non hanno nulla di visivamente spettacolare ma che sotto la superficie ribollono di un senso di scoperta, di ribellione e di unicità. Gli anni novanta del rock alternativo sono stati descritti attraverso le fotografie dei grandi concerti, le copertine dei dischi, i video musicali trasmessi da Mtv e soprattutto i ritratti-santino di musicisti morti troppo giovani.

Le fotografie di Auf der Maur ci mostrano invece il disordine che c’era intorno a tutto questo: camere d’albergo squallide, bicchieri sporchi, telefoni che oggi ci sembrano anticaglie da museo, televisori minuscoli, vestiti e biancheria lasciati ad asciugare nei bagni. Nel saggio che accompagna il libro, la critica musicale Ann Powers parla di jolie laide, una bellezza irregolare e un po’ sgraziata: “Cosa significa guardare un gran casino e non vederci un disastro ma bellezza, un senso di possibilità e di vita incontenibile?”.

“Vita incontenibile”, ecco una definizione che si adatta bene alla cultura e all’estetica grunge, che aveva trasformato abiti usati, capelli sporchi e una certa trascuratezza in una specie di manifesto estetico e che aveva ridato centralità al corpo, alla mischia nel moshpit, agli ormoni incontrollabili, ai fluidi corporali e agli odori che gli anni ottanta avevano cercato di coprire e di addomesticare sotto una patina di glamour e di egoismo. Quella trascuratezza, prima di essere recuperata dalla moda, apparteneva a una cultura indipendente che aveva fatto del rifiuto delle convenzioni e del successo commerciale una parte importante della propria identità.

Dai margini al centro

Negli anni novanta tutto questo stava cambiando. Con il successo dei Nirvana, delle Hole e degli Smashing Pumpkins, una cultura nata ai margini dell’industria musicale si era ritrovata improvvisamente al centro. Auf der Maur ha fotografato proprio quel passaggio: il momento in cui l’underground diventava mainstream e un mondo che fino a poco prima si era retto su piccole etichette, fanzine e concerti organizzati tra amici entrava nel tritacarne del rock internazionale.

C’è un altro aspetto che mi colpisce in queste fotografie. Auf der Maur scatta molto dal palco e il pubblico ha quasi sempre le mani vuote. Qualcuno tiene un accendino, qualcuno un cartello fatto a mano o agita una maglietta sudata come una bandiera, gli altri alzano semplicemente le braccia. Nessuno sta riprendendo il concerto con il telefono perché gli smartphone semplicemente non estivano ancora.

Auf der Maur fotografava in continuazione: sfogliando il libro si ha l’impressione che in qualche modo sapesse e che cercasse di raccogliere più momenti possibili, più sensazioni possibili. Non c’è motivo di pensare che negli anni novanta le persone fossero più autentiche o vivessero più intensamente il presente o la musica. La differenza è che quelle fotografie non erano destinate a essere condivise o viste immediatamente da qualcuno. Bisognava finire un rullino, portarlo a sviluppare, aspettare di vedere le immagini. Molte finivano in un album o in una scatola e potevano restare lì per anni.

Oggi documentare la propria vita e renderla pubblica sono diventate due attività quasi inseparabili. Negli anni novanta esisteva ancora uno spazio abbastanza ampio tra quello che facevamo e l’immagine che decidevamo di dare di noi stessi. Molto spesso quello che eravamo la notte in un locale o a un concerto era qualcosa di molto diverso da quello che cercavamo di essere di giorno. Esisteva una specie di intimità nella folla, un senso di caloroso anonimato che oggi sarebbe molto difficile da spiegare.

Naturalmente non era un mondo migliore. Auf der Maur nel suo memoir ricorda quanto fosse maschilista l’ambiente del rock alternativo e quanto fosse difficile per una donna, soprattutto per una donna come Courtney Love, muoversi in un’industria che continuava a giudicare le artiste secondo regole molto diverse da quelle riservate agli uomini.

Le fotografie raccontano anche un’epoca segnata dalle dipendenze, dalla violenza e dalla rapida trasformazione di una controcultura in un prodotto commerciale. Auf der Maur scattava fotografie per ricordare e per capire quello che le stava succedendo. La sua piccola Nikon era una specie di protezione, un amuleto, contro il caos che la circondava.

articles.title: La economía china acelera su crecimiento al 4,5% en el tercer trimestre
articles.summary: El tirón exportador sostiene el avance del PIB, mientras Pekín reconoce la debilidad de la demanda interna y la inversión inmobiliaria sigue cayendo
articles.preview: El empuje de las exportaciones y el repunte de la actividad industrial han permitido a China acelerar su crecimiento en el tercer trimestre de 2026, a pesar de la debilidad del consumo y la caída de la inversión. El producto interior bruto (PIB) creció un 4,5% interanual entre julio y septiembre, dos décimas más que en el trimestre anterior, según los datos publicados este lunes por la Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas (ONE).
articles.body:
El empuje de las exportaciones y el repunte de la actividad industrial han permitido a China acelerar su crecimiento en el tercer trimestre de 2026, a pesar de la debilidad del consumo y la caída de la inversión. El producto interior bruto (PIB) creció un 4,5% interanual entre julio y septiembre, dos décimas más que en el trimestre anterior, según los datos publicados este lunes por la Oficina Nacional de Estadísticas (ONE).

La economía china había registrado entre abril y junio el ritmo de expansión más bajo desde finales de 2022 , pese a haber crecido un 5% interanual en los tres primeros meses del año. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
articles.summary: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.
articles.preview: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history. On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.
articles.body:
France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.

On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.

An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.

There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.

Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail.

How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account?

How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time?

Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated?

And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education?

On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France.

He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests.

The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why.

"Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night.

Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines.

That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets.

Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks.

Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets.

What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment.

People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation.

Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility.

"While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me.

Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented".

For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday.

But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests.

France is holding its breath.

articles.body:
US president accuses Ukrainian leader of not wanting to end the war, as Zelenskyy speaks with Washington envoys.

United States President Donald Trump has defended sanction waivers for Russia, saying he wants to keep Moscow at the bargaining table and accusing his counterpart in Kyiv of not wanting to end the war in Ukraine.

Trump made the comments on Truth Social on Sunday in response to criticism of his decision to block numerous sanctions on Russia just days before they were due to take effect.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he said.

The move has triggered a significant diplomatic fallout between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the past week.

Zelenskyy said that waiving sanctions on Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, “will hurt Ukraine”, telling NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that it would strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

“We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s [an] aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist, and that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”

Trump reiterated his claim that Zelenskyy does not want the war on his country to end, saying on Truth Social that Kyiv was launching attacks on diesel refineries in Russia despite knowing it was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets”.

“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him… he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote.

Trump announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched war on Iran in late February. The move led Tehran to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global energy exports transited before the war.

Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against Ukraine.

US-Ukraine talks continue

The Ukrainian president said on X on Sunday that he has spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of “virtually non-stop communication” between the two countries’ teams aimed at the “next steps in diplomacy”.

“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Zelenskyy spoke with Witkoff and Kushner as Russia and Ukraine continued to strike each other’s energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power, and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Russia, in St Petersburg, since the war began.

articles.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
articles.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
articles.preview: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table". Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".

Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.

Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.

The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.

Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.

However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.

Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

articles.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
articles.summary: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.
articles.preview: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities. The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit. Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes.
articles.body:
At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.

The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.

A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.

Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.

Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.

It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.

Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.

Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.

St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.

He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.

Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.

Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.

It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".

As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.

Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.

Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.

However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps.

Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.

Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.

Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.

Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

articles.title: Gli album da ascoltare
articles.summary: Da Dopamine chamber dei Fontaines D.C a Dja dja di Marina Herlop. Le recensioni della stampa straniera
articles.preview: Con il disco precedente, Romance, i Fontaines D.C. avevano trasformato il loro post-punk in qualcosa di più audace e spettacolare. Dopamine chamber, quinto album della band di Dublino, porta quella metamorfosi alle estreme conseguenze e sembra raggiungere quello che il gruppo inseguiva da tempo: le chitarre cedono spazio all’elettronica, agli archi cinematografici e ad atmosfere gotiche.
articles.body:
Con il disco precedente, Romance, i Fontaines D.C. avevano trasformato il loro post-punk in qualcosa di più audace e spettacolare. Dopamine chamber, quinto album della band di Dublino, porta quella metamorfosi alle estreme conseguenze e sembra raggiungere quello che il gruppo inseguiva da tempo: le chitarre cedono spazio all’elettronica, agli archi cinematografici e ad atmosfere gotiche. Dopamine chamber esplora il lato più cupo della contemporaneità, dalla dipendenza dagli smartphone (evocati nel titolo dell’album) al collasso ambientale, dalle disuguaglianze alla violenza politica. Il brano d’apertura Six shot morning e il singolo Marianne colpiscono per intensità, sostenuti da arrangiamenti imponenti e dalla voce tesa del cantante Grian Chatten, che è anche il principale paroliere della band. Mimesis offre una parentesi pop, mentre in Tongue Chatten sfoggia un testo ricco costruito su un sottofondo di percussioni delicate, una sezione d’archi e una linea di basso e un motivo di pianoforte ispirati ai Wu-Tang Clan e ai Mobb Deep. Japan guarda agli Arctic Monkeys di Humbug e promette cori da stadio ai concerti; in Where is gone? la cantante spagnola Rosalía accompagna Chatten in una ballata che sembra quasi la colonna sonora di un film di James Bond. Tra echi di Nino Rota, Mina, Massive Attack e Portishead, i Fontaines D.C. costruiscono il loro lavoro più ambizioso: un universo sonoro mutevole, dove melodie splendide convivono con inquietudini profonde e contemporanee. La vastità di Romance non ha fatto che accrescersi: con questo, il quintetto irlandese si è dedicato a un’esplorazione sonora a tutto tondo di quello che sono i Fontaines D.C. E anche di quello che potrebbero diventare in futuro.

James Mellen, Clash

A volte sembra che la musica venga creata senza sforzi; altre sembra che sia frutto di un processo massacrante. Il quinto album della brillante Marina Herlop appartiene alla seconda categoria. Finora l’artista catalana non ha mai nascosto la complessità del suo lavoro, che porta la musica classica in territori di pop alieno. Ma Dja dja è ambizioso perfino per lei: in quindici brani intensi combina trame vocali articolate con percussioni marziali, ticchettii, versi di uccelli mutanti e bassi organici. Sembra la ricetta perfetta per un mal di testa, ma come dimostrano l’estasi cinematica di Bliss o il jazz funk scoppiettante di Vas volant qui ci sono bellezza, divertimento e ritmo mentre Herlop segue la sua musa attraverso un labirinto d’ispirazione, come una Björk dell’Europa del sud o una Fever Ray che abbia davvero la febbre.

Ben Cardew, Dj Mag

Questa raccolta è il frutto delle ricerche condotte da Susan Tomes per un suo libro dedicato alle pianiste nel corso della storia. Come ha scoperto l’autrice, molte di loro componevano anche musica, brevi brani destinati ai salotti e alle cerchie domestiche a cui erano spesso confinate. Alcune delle dodici donne qui presentate sono famose, ma molte vi saranno nuove. Un esempio è Marianne Martínez, che riceveva lezioni in cambio dell’affitto dall’inquilino di famiglia, Haydn: la sua sonata in la maggiore ha lo splendore di Scarlatti. Marianna von Auenbrugger morì a 23 anni, ma fu allieva di Salieri, che finanziò la pubblicazione della sua mozartiana sonata in mi bemolle maggiore. La musica di Clara Schumann, Fanny Mendelssohn e Cécile Chaminade non ha bisogno di presentazioni, ma vale la pena di conoscere la virtuosa polacca Maria Agata Szymanowska, il cui Caprice sur la romance de Joconde fu dedicato al suo vicino di casa a San Pietroburgo, John Field. O la pianista venezuelana Teresa Carreño, il cui Un bal en rêve ricorda Happy birthday, che arrivò un quarto di secolo dopo. L’album non sarebbe così bello se non fosse per Tomes: il suo tocco poetico e sensibile offre a questa musica raffinata la possibilità di esprimersi al meglio.

Clive Paget, The Guardian

articles.title: Bomb threat forces Israel to Austria flight into emergency landing
articles.summary: The Airbus jet landed safely in Bulgaria and all passengers and crew aboard were unharmed, officials said.
articles.preview: An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria was forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat. The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement. The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the statement said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun.
articles.body:
An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria was forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat.

The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement.

The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the statement said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun.

It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight's crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made.

Austrian Airlines confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the BBC there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet.

Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia.

Austrian Airlines confirmed that no threat was found and the flight finished its journey to Vienna with all passengers on board.

Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later.

Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.

articles.title: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
articles.summary: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
articles.preview: One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages. Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.
articles.body:
One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.

Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.

The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.

One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.

Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.

Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.

"It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat."

"This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.

The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."

Already, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.

The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.

Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, violence has continued, including almost daily Israeli strikes, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.

There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.

Families currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets.

"The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".

The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."

There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food.

"It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."

Humanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.

In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".

For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.

In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September.

The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.

articles.title: The kingmakers who could determine Israel’s election
articles.summary: Israel’s Arab-led and ultra-Orthodox parties face attacks but could hold the balance of power after October 27 vote.
articles.preview: Israel’s Arab-led and ultra-Orthodox parties face attacks but could hold the balance of power after October 27 vote. In the run-up to Israel’s high-stakes election, few parties have featured more often in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attacks on rivals than Ra’am and the Joint List. Together, the two parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats.
articles.body:
Israel’s Arab-led and ultra-Orthodox parties face attacks but could hold the balance of power after October 27 vote.

In the run-up to Israel’s high-stakes election, few parties have featured more often in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attacks on rivals than Ra’am and the Joint List.

Together, the two parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats. If this is confirmed at the October 27 polls, the Arab-led lists could be critical to any post-election coalition, regardless of its political stripe.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

- list 1 of 4What ‘right’ and ‘left’ mean in Israel today

- list 2 of 4Israel election double standard: Arab leader forced out, far right cleared

- list 3 of 4Israel’s Netanyahu criticises opposition uniting against him for elections

- list 4 of 4Israel’s Supreme Court advises Arab party leader to drop election bid

They have been here before.

In 2021, Ra’am made history by becoming the first Arab party to enter an Israeli government after joining a broad coalition that briefly removed Netanyahu from power. Netanyahu had previously shown himself ready to negotiate terms for a potential government with Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List. But instead, Abbas joined forces with the coalition of Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid to try to drive through some of the measures he had campaigned for.

This time, both the Netanyahu camp and most leaders of the self-styled Zionist opposition bloc have ruled out forming a government with the parties representing Palestinian citizens. Still, Netanyahu and his allies have sought to portray their political opponents as beholden to the Arab-led lists, while the opposition has been attacking them for their reliance on the minority ultra-Orthodox parties to maintain their own power base.

Opinion polls have consistently indicated that Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads are running neck-and-neck with the Zionist opposition bloc, with neither side on track to win an outright majority in the 120-strong Knesset.

“Netanyahu would work with Ra’am in a heartbeat, if it meant staying in power,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a Middle East analyst at Chatham House.

“The opposition, too, don’t seem to understand the consequences of their actions,” he said of repeated attempts across the opposition bloc to undermine the credibility of what may be a future plank in any government.

“If it came down to it, of course they’d accept the support of the party they’d previously vilified without thinking of how that will undermine their government, and undermine the votes of the large numbers of Arab Israelis who support them,” added Mekelberg.

In the lead-up to the polls, Likud has repeatedly used hard-hitting attack adverts to warn that if Netanyahu is voted out, it will be the Arab parties that would emerge as kingmakers in a new government potentially led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party.

“There is no Gadi without [Ahmad] Tibi,” said a Likud campaign slogan in reference to the leader of Ta’al, one of three parties comprising the Joint List.

The alliance, which also includes the Hadash and Balad factions, has said it could provide a so-called safety net to the anti-Netanyahu coalition by agreeing not to stand against it in a confidence vote, even if the alliance does not join the government. In return, it has said it would demand certain conditions, including a path to Palestinian statehood and fighting organised crime.

Combatting the wave of violent crime that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities, as well as addressing discriminatory government policies, including on housing, have also been the focus of Ra’am ahead of the election.

Established in 1996, the party has already distanced itself from its religiously conservative foundations. In December 2025, Abbas said the party’s political decision-making body would separate from its religious council. Eight months later, it selected its electoral list independently for the first time and placed the Jewish Zionist Yoav Segalovitz, a former senior police commander and deputy public security minister in the Bennett-Lapid government, second on its slate.

Describing Ra’am as “one of the most interesting parties” of this year’s election, Mekelberg said: “Through Mansour Abbas, they are continually reinventing themselves without appearing opportunist.”

The upcoming election is the first since the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel of October 7, 2023 that led to the killing of an estimated 1,200 people, and triggered Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

The war has also sped up a political shift to the right, with Arab-led parties increasingly targeted by right-wing figures seeking to cast them as complicit in the October 7 assault.

In May, Bennett apologised for going into government with Ra’am, while in September, Netanyahu’s Likud and the Otzma Yehudi party of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir petitioned to bar Ra’am and the Joint List from the election.

On September 23, the Central Elections Committee, whose members are drawn from the Knesset’s parties, voted to disqualify both lists, as well as two individual candidates.

Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh was to be barred over an article he wrote on October 8, 2023 describing the Hamas-led attack of the previous day as an “important historic event”. Ofer Cassif, a Jewish politician with Hadash, was targeted in a petition filed by Likud that cited legal prohibitions on candidates who support “an armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organisation against the State of Israel”.

On October 2, the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the disqualifications of the Joint List and Ra’am, as well as Cassif’s, by a 7-2 majority. Abu Shehadeh had withdrawn his candidacy a day earlier, after it became clear the court was likely to uphold his disqualification.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Cassif later called it “a political decision far more than a judicial one”, driven by “fear that they’re going to need us”.

Orly Noy, a Balad candidate and the first Jewish politician to be voted onto the party list’s top five, said it was “safe to say” that the alliance is not going to be part of the next ruling coalition.

“It depends if the other parties want to prioritise the wishes of their voters or their own racism. However, even if we’re excluded, we can still gain concessions from any coalition in return for our support,” she added. “That might not mean ending the occupation, which of course would be ideal, but there’s a lot we can still do that will make people’s lives better.”

Fallout

The taint of October 7 has not only extended to Arab parties unconnected to the events of that day, but also to ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

As routine partners in Likud’s governing coalitions, they have faced accusations by many leading opponents of draft-dodging, while drawing heavily on what many regard as a generous state welfare package.

Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community is largely represented by two parties: Shas, which draws on Jews of Spanish, North African and Middle Eastern descent; and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), comprising Jews of central and eastern European descent. Each is polling at about seven or eight seats.

Rather than focusing on foreign policy and taxation, their core aims tend to be shielding ultra-Orthodox students from military service, securing welfare support for the large families common in the community, where many men study rather than work, and protecting state funding for their schools and institutions.

Long seen as Netanyahu’s most dependable allies, they broke with Likud last year over its failure to legislate an exemption to the draft. The UTJ left the coalition altogether, while Shas quit the government but did not pull its 11 politicians out of the parliamentary coalition. Shas later gave up its coalition committee roles, and both parties boycotted coalition bills.

Nevertheless, the support of the ultra-Orthodox has come with a political price tag. In January, opposition leader Yair Lapid accused the government of sending billions “to the corrupt and [the] draft dodgers” while another possible contender for the premiership, the right-wing Avigdor Lieberman, who heads the Yisrael Beytenu list, likened Shas and UTJ to the Taliban over their lack of female representation.

articles.title: Ukraine launches over 1,000 drones at Russia, setting oil facilities ablaze
articles.summary: The air strike, one of Ukraine's largest in the war, comes amid rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
articles.preview: The air strike, one of Ukraine’s largest in the war, comes amid rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington. At least one person has been killed, and five others injured after Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, one of Kyiv’s largest aerial strikes in the war. St Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said firefighters were battling fires sparked by Sunday’s attacks on the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky district south of the city.
articles.body:
The air strike, one of Ukraine’s largest in the war, comes amid rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington.

At least one person has been killed, and five others injured after Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, one of Kyiv’s largest aerial strikes in the war.

St Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said firefighters were battling fires sparked by Sunday’s attacks on the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky district south of the city.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that?

- list 2 of 3Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing

- list 3 of 3Photos: Protests across France spiral into looting, blazes and clashes

The governor said the “massive” strike killed at least one person and injured five, and that several residential buildings and two houses were also hit.

The attack disrupted flights at St Petersburg’s main airport, one of the country’s busiest, which was restricting operations “for safety reasons”, Beglov said.

Russian e-commerce company Ozon said there was a fire at its logistics hub in St Petersburg. The internet company VK said drones attacked its data centre in the broader Leningrad region, adding that normal services were available to users.

Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity following the drone raid.

The Ministry of Defence said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

US-Ukraine tensions deepen

The strikes came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepened, with US President Donald Trump criticising Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, and the prospect of further US sanctions against Moscow still uncertain.

On Sunday, Trump defended his Friday decision to put a hold on implementing new sanctions on Russia, saying he did not want to do anything that would “foolishly” drive Moscow “away from the bargaining table”.

In a social media post, the US president said he believed new sanctions would undermine negotiations to bring about a diplomatic end to Moscow’s war on Ukraine, refuting bipartisan criticism that he was favouring Russian President Vladimir Putin’s interests over Kyiv’s.

Trump also lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has been critical of Trump’s recent outreach to Putin, for launching strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, claiming Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war”.

Trump had announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, but offered no details. Zelenskyy told The Financial Times that he was “done” with the ceasefire a few days later, after holding off on striking Russia’s energy facilities while Moscow had continued attacking Ukraine’s.

Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump’s announcement.

Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to “cause a blackout”.

“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said.

Speaking on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin’s war effort. He also said US-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being “blocked for some period of time”.

Zelenskyy said that while he trusted Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a “historic mistake” for Washington.

Later on Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an October 9 meeting between Washington and Kyiv’s negotiating teams in Miami, as well as the “next steps in diplomacy”.

Russian strikes kill two

Meanwhile, a Russian air strike killed a woman in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, overnight while also hitting a subway station and damaging a 25-storey residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.

The attack, which also hit non-residential buildings and a medical facility, injured three other people in Kyiv, Klitschko said.

Two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed a woman and wounded at least two other people, including a six-year-old girl, local officials said on Sunday.

In another post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian strikes on residential buildings had killed two people and injured 12, including two children, in Volyn.

“This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said.

“In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
articles.preview: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia. One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil. He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
articles.body:
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.

One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.

He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.

The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.

There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."

And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.

It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia.

- If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.

"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.

His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.

"When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.

He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.

If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.

"You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".

But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.

Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.

Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.

"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."

But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

"Putin won't live forever," he said.

articles.title: La storia del crollo dei bot russi dopo gli attacchi ucraini a Yandex è priva di riscontri
articles.summary: Si è molto diffusa online in questi giorni, ma analisi indipendenti hanno mostrato che non esistono dati per confermarla
articles.preview: Altri osservatori, basandosi su proprie analisi, hanno invece sostenuto che, dopo l’attacco ai server russi di Yandex, i contenuti legati alle campagna di disinformazione russa che prendono di mira tematiche come le prossime elezioni presidenziali francesi avrebbero ottenuto su X solo poche decine di migliaia di visualizzazioni. A settembre, prima dei droni ucraini, questi contenuti ne avrebbero ottenute milioni.
articles.body:
Altri osservatori, basandosi su proprie analisi, hanno invece sostenuto che, dopo l’attacco ai server russi di Yandex, i contenuti legati alle campagna di disinformazione russa che prendono di mira tematiche come le prossime elezioni presidenziali francesi avrebbero ottenuto su X solo poche decine di migliaia di visualizzazioni. A settembre, prima dei droni ucraini, questi contenuti ne avrebbero ottenute milioni.

Verifiche indipendenti e molti esperti di disinformazione hanno spiegato tuttavia che non esistono ad oggi dati affidabili e verificabili che dimostrino che ci sia stato un calo significativo dell’attività di influenza russa online dopo l’attacco ucraino alle infrastrutture di Yandex.

Cosa dicono le analisi e le indagini indipendenti

Da più parti si è provato subito a fare chiarezza su come andassero interpretati i grafici utilizzati come prova. L’istituto di monitoraggio dei media polacco Emocje w slacieci ha chiarito innanzitutto un concetto, la cui scarsa conoscenza ha favorito il diffondersi di questa narrazione: un bot non è necessariamente un account falso che diffonde propaganda del Cremlino sui social media. Inoltre, nel caso dell’attacco ai server di Yandex, a essere rilevato era stato il crollo dell’attività dei cosiddetti web crawler, ossia i programmi automatici impiegati da ogni motore di ricerca, incluso quello russo di Yandex, per esplorare il web e per indicizzarne i contenuti. La stessa Cloudflare, riporta la BBC, ha chiarito che i suoi dati includono tutte le richieste Internet automatizzate ai siti web ospitati sulla sua rete, compresi i bot che scansionano i siti web alla ricerca di informazioni. L’azienda statunitense ha inoltre specificato all’emittente pubblica che il calo mostrato nel grafico «non è necessariamente dovuto al comportamento dei bot sulle piattaforme dei social media».

Il secondo grafico, invece, quello che avrebbe mostrato il crollo delle attività online riguardanti AfD dopo gli attacchi ucraini, risulta essere privo di qualsiasi riscontro. Il grafico in questione infatti, oltre a non aver alcuna fonte indicata sulla provenienza dei dati e a non risultare chiaro nella dicitura “attività giornaliera”, risulta essere stato pubblicato su Threads per la prima volta l’11 ottobre. Tuttavia, nell’asse orizzontale del diagramma i dati arrivano fino al “15 ottobre”, quindi una data futura.

Agli esperti di disinformazione l’idea che un semplice attacco di questo tipo potesse portare a un crollo delle operazioni di influenza russa è suonata subito molto semplicistica: parlando col Guardian, Ned Mendez, responsabile della ricerca dell’organizzazione Alliance4Europe che si batte contro la disinformazione, ha spiegato che per evitare di essere segnalate come sospette dalle piattaforme, le bot farm operano con modalità che ne favoriscono la distribuzione e la resilienza, per esempio attraverso connessioni residenziali e phone farm. «Non possiamo semplicemente cancellare i bot a forza di bombe, per quanto l’idea possa sembrare allettante», ha dichiarato Mendez.

Vari istituti che analizzano la disinformazione online hanno invece segnalato che, dal canto loro, non era stata individuata nessuna correlazione tra l’attacco ai data center di Yandex e un crollo del traffico di certi account. Come riportato dalla testata tedesca Capital, sia l’Istituto di ricerca Cemas che il think tank Polisphere – entrambi impegnati nell’analisi di disinformazione e nel monitoraggio social di account tedeschi attribuibili ad attori della disinformazione, sostenitori dell’AfD e gruppi di diffusori filoruss – non si sono registrati cali statisticamente significativi dell’attività nei Paesi di lingua tedesca. Sono state dello stesso tenore le affermazioni di altri analisti e del gruppo BotBlocker, specializzato nell’analisi di troll farm russe presenti sulle piattaforme social.

Quando le affermazioni categoriche delle prime ore sono state messe in discussione, non trovando conferme indipendenti, alcuni dei profili che più avevano contribuito a diffondere questa narrazione sono intervenuti di nuovo per scusarsi o ridimensionare la propria posizione iniziale. L’analista militare polacco Jaroslav Wolski che aveva postato il grafico infondato su AfD ha cancellato il tweet e scritto un secondo post sull’argomento: «Purtroppo il mio post contenente disinformazione ha raggiunto milioni di visualizzazioni, e per questo desidero scusarmi ancora una volta con tutti i lettori. Naturalmente mi assumo la piena responsabilità di ciò che ho fatto e, in modo semplice e umano, mi vergogno di avervi disinformato. Chiedo scusa anche agli oppositori che avevo contestato e che sono stati i primi a farmi notare che mi sbagliavo».

Mentre in risposta a una richiesta di informazioni da parte di ZDFheute, l’eurodeputato ceco Zdechovský ha ammesso di non possedere attualmente dati verificabili in modo indipendente che provino in modo definitivo un collegamento tra gli attacchi e un calo dell’attività delle reti di disinformazione russe. «Non ho mai affermato che tale collegamento sia stato definitivamente dimostrato», ha aggiunto.

L’ufficio di Zelensky ha dichiarato alla BBC che il presidente ucraino si riferiva «all’atmosfera sui social media» piuttosto che a una diminuzione dell’attività dei bot, aggiungendo di aver ricevuto «segnalazioni di un minor numero di commenti provocatori e di incitamento all’odio» da parte di molti utenti dei social media.

Le conseguenze provate degli attacchi ucraini

Come abbiamo visto, quindi, non ci sono prove che permettano di concludere che gli attacchi ai data center di Yandex abbiano avuto un impatto sulle operazioni di influenza della Russia. Ma questo non significa che non ci siano state conseguenze in Russia.

Come scrive Meduza – media russo indipendente con sede in Lettonia, bloccato in Russia perché considerato «organizzazione indesiderabile» – i droni ucraini hanno creato interruzioni diffuse su tutta la rete internet russa, bloccando temporaneamente i servizi di Yandex, tra cui Yandex Go, Yandex Eats e Yandex Pay, utilizzati in gran numero di russi. Inoltre, molti altri siti web e servizi sono andati offline, tra cui quelli di importanti banche, rivenditori, marketplace online, piattaforme di annunci classificati, siti web e app di notizie e molto altro. Questo perché queste aziende utilizzavano l’infrastruttura di Yandex per archiviare i propri dati. I russi, inoltre, continua Meduza, hanno perso l’accesso a una serie di servizi di uso quotidiano, come chiamare un taxi, effettuare pagamenti, ordinare consegne, controllare la posta elettronica. Fino al 13 ottobre, la stessa Yandex aveva comunicato ai propri utenti di star continuando a lavorare per ripristinare il funzionamento completo delle proprie attività.

Il Financial Times riporta che i disagi si sono estesi anche ai paesi confinanti con la Russia, con interruzioni dei servizi di posta elettronica, Yandex Pay e siti web che utilizzano l’infrastruttura dell’azienda russa in Kazakistan, Uzbekistan e Bielorussia. Nel 2024 Yandex era stata venduta forzatamente a investitori legati al presidente russo Vladimir Putin. All’epoca il vicepresidente della commissione parlamentare russa sull’informazione, Anton Gorelkin, aveva detto che «Yandex è più di un’azienda, è una risorsa per l’intera società russa».

articles.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
articles.summary: The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a blockbuster stock market listing.
articles.preview: Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good". The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn).

The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market.

None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added.

Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday.

Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as â60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".

In a blog post, Anthropic said it was committing 5 percent of company shares with immediate effect, subject to stockholder approval, with an additional 2 percent to be added “at the board’s discretion” for every 50 percent increase in the company’s value.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the San Francisco-based firm said.

Anthropic, officially registered as a “public benefit corporation” in the US state of Delaware, said the fund would not be used for lobbying or political donations, either in the United States or overseas.

Founded in 2021 by former employees of ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Anthropic is preparing for what could be the largest public initial offering in history. It is expected to list on the US stock market before the end of 2026, with analysts forecasting a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.

The company’s charter requires its leadership to balance shareholder returns with responsible AI development.
